newsitem.title: USA: Europe/Japan rate prospects may hinder mark/yen.
newsitem.headline: Europe/Japan rate prospects may hinder mark/yen.

text.p: With prospects for higher German interest rates even more remote than chances for a rise in Japanese rates, currency experts expect only limited gains for the buoyant mark/yen cross going forward.
Mark/yen scaled 73.50 for the first time in five weeks on Wednesday -- up from a recent low of 70.45 in early March -- but analysts said they expect the advance to sputter before too long.

"We are looking for the market to start pricing in some firmer rates in Japan sooner, so I guess over time you have to give mark/yen a slightly downward bias," said Ron Leven, international strategist at J.P. Morgan.

On Wednesday, Bank of Japan (BOJ) Governor Yasuo Matsushita dispelled some notions that Japan's paltry interest rates would rise in the foreseeable future, highlighting the yen's glaring yield disadvantage after the Federal Reserve executed its first rate hike in two years on Tuesday.

The Japanese unit slumped broadly, in part because his remarks implied that speculation by some currency traders that U.S./Japan interest rate differentials were going to tighten was misplaced, analysts said.
While delivering an upbeat assessment of Japan's economy at a news conference, the BOJ chief ruled out a change to its easy credit policy.
Matsushita said the planned implementation of a sales tax increase next month to five percent from three percent would inevitably slow Japanese growth temporarily.
BOJ monetary policy will focus on Japan's domestic economy and will not be directly influenced by the Fed's quarter-point increase in the federal funds target rate on Tuesday, he added.

The Japanese central bank has kept the official discount rate which it charges commercial banks at a record low 0.5 percent since September 1995 to help economic recovery and facilitate Japanese banks' disposal of non-performing loans.

"Right now the yen is sort of trading heavy because it looks like the fiscal package is going to go through," Leven said. "I think it was also some expectations built up that the securitization of the real estate market was going to radically change problems of the banking system, which it won't."
But despite nagging concerns about Japan's economy, it nonetheless appears to be outpacing Europe's core economies.
Although Germany has shown sporadic signs of recovery, it could be a relatively longer wait before the Bundesbank snugs its monetary policy, economists said.
"It's not apparent to me there are more pressures on Germany to start tightening than there are on Japan," said John Rothfield, international economist at Nationsbanc-CRT.
"After all, Japan has had at least a year of strong economic growth, ... over three percent in last four quarters, and that has been significantly stronger than the German economy," he continued.
Germany has shown signs of improved manufacturing activity and higher retail sales in the last couple of months, economists said.
But it will take some time for nascent improvements in the factory sector to lower Germany's record high unemployment rate, they added.
Furthermore, there was bad news when Germany's engineering industry association showed on Thursday that February plant and machinery orders fell 0.6 percent from a year ago.

In the meantime German interest rates, especially the repo, its main money market rate, could be held captive to changes in the jobs market, economists said. The repo has stood at 3.0 percent since August, when the Bundesbank trimmed the rate from 3.3 percent.

"The labor market is not going to improve significantly and our past studies have shown that the Bundesbank repo rate has changed most responsively to changes in unemployment in West Germany," Rothfield said.
